footer.description: Real-time audio collaboration and secure demo sharing platform for music producers.

problem.title: Sending a demo shouldn't cost you the track.
problem.lead: Two things break every remote review: the file leaves your hands, and nobody hears the same second.

leak.label: Problem 01
leak.title: The file walks
leak.body: A WAV in an inbox is a WAV on somebody else's drive. Once it has been downloaded there is no version, no owner, and no way back.
leak.answer: Every master carries your voice, and every link expires.

drift.label: Problem 02
drift.title: The room drifts
drift.body: One person pauses, another seeks, a third hears the drop four seconds late. Notes stop being about the music and start being about timecode.
drift.answer: One playhead, one position, broadcast to the whole room.

pillars.title: Three modules, one workbench.
pillars.lead: A library that holds the work, a tag that signs it, and a room to play it in.

library.title: Library
library.description: Upload MP3, WAV or FLAC straight to storage and keep every take in one place.

voiceTag.title: Voice Tag
voiceTag.description: Write it or record it, then bake it into the master on a loop you control.
voiceTag.fact2: Or upload your own, up to 10s

liveRoom.title: Live Room
liveRoom.description: Share a six-character code and listen together, in step, with voice on top.
liveRoom.fact1: Play, pause and seek stay in sync

voiceTag.title: Your name, every thirty seconds.
voiceTag.lead: The tag is mixed into the master on the server, not layered on in the player — so what leaves the platform is already signed.
voiceTag.point1Body: Wavenet and Neural2 voices in Vietnamese, US English and UK English, male or female. Or upload a take of your own, up to ten seconds.
voiceTag.point2Title: Hear it before you keep it
voiceTag.point2Body: Preview any wording and voice together. Nothing is stored until you decide to save it.
voiceTag.point3Body: FFmpeg loops the tag, ducks the music underneath it and exports a new MP3 master. The settings are fixed at upload, so the result is reproducible.

liveRoom.title: Everyone on the same bar.
liveRoom.lead: The host holds the transport. Play, pause, seek and track changes go out over WebSocket, so the room hears one position — not five.
liveRoom.point1Body: Share a six-character code. Requests land in a waiting room, and nobody is inside until you let them in.
liveRoom.point2Body: Comments attach to a position on the timeline and surface as playback reaches them. No more “around 1:42, I think”.
liveRoom.point3Body: Peer-to-peer voice and video for up to seven people, negotiated through the server and carried directly between browsers.
liveRoom.commentSample: the low end fights the kick here

workflow.title: From upload to listening party in four moves.
workflow.step1Body: The file goes straight from your browser to storage over a signed, one-hour link. You watch a progress bar, not a spinner.
workflow.step2Body: Pick a voice tag, then set the interval, volume, ducking and start offset. Locked in at upload so the master stays reproducible.
workflow.step3Body: The job is queued and picked up by a worker that mixes the tag in with FFmpeg. Follow it from processing to ready — and retry if it fails.
workflow.step4Body: Open a room, send the code, approve who joins and press play. Everyone hears the same second.

trust.title: Boring where it matters.
trust.lead: The parts nobody puts in a demo, built anyway.
trust.item1Body: Every storage key is checked against the account that owns it before a file is read or written.
trust.item2Body: Playback runs on signed URLs valid from one minute to twenty-four hours, and they cannot be reused after that.
trust.item3Body: Refresh tokens rotate on every use, revoked ones are blacklisted, and you can end any active session yourself.
trust.item4Body: Closed accounts are anonymised by a scheduled job, and deleting a track clears its files from storage too.

cta.headline: Put your next demo in a room.
cta.subheadline: Create an account, upload a track and share the code. It takes about a minute.
cta.footnote: Free to start · Nothing to install

hero.title: Three modules, walked through step by step.
hero.lead: Every module below is the real flow, in the order the screens appear: what you click, what the app asks for, and what comes back. The illustrations are captured from the running app.
hero.techLink: Or read how it is built underneath

voiceTag.title: Create a voice tag, end to end.
voiceTag.lead: A voice tag is the audio signature stamped over your demos. This is the whole path: from opening the tab to a saved tag waiting in the picker.

open.title: Open the Voice Tags tab
open.body: Sign in, then go to Dashboard → Voice Tags. Every tag you own lives here and plays straight from the list. The first time, the list is empty and offers a single button: Create.
open.note: Voice Tags is a Pro module. On a free account the list is replaced by an upgrade prompt.
open.mediaHint: The Voice Tags tab in its empty state, with the Create button.

create.title: Press Create and pick a method
create.body: Two cards, one choice: let a synthetic voice read a line you type, or upload a clip you recorded yourself. Nothing is locked in — you can come back and make another tag the other way.
create.mediaHint: The two creation cards: Generate with AI (TTS) and Upload your own audio.

fork.title: Fill in the branch you chose
fork.body: The two methods ask for different things, and only the one you picked needs finishing.

tts.title: Generate with a synthetic voice
tts.body: Name the tag, type the line to be spoken, then choose a language and a voice. Switching language clears the voice, because each language carries its own set.
tts.mediaHint: The TTS form with the language and voice dropdowns open.

voice.label: Voice
voice.value: Male or female, or the system default

upload.title: Upload a clip you recorded
upload.body: Drop a file into the box or click to choose one. The name is filled in from the filename, and stays yours the moment you edit it. The browser reads the duration before anything is sent, so an over-length clip is refused without spending bandwidth.
upload.mediaHint: Dropping a file into the dropzone: the duration read back, and the inline player underneath.

preview.title: Listen before you save
preview.body: Preview synthesises a sample from exactly what the form holds right now. Nothing is stored yet — leave at this point and no tag exists. Change the text, the language or the voice and the old sample is dropped, so you never judge a stale one.
preview.note: Previews are rate limited. Past the ceiling the app tells you how many seconds to wait before the next one.
preview.mediaHint: Short clip: pressing Preview, the loader, then the sample playing.

scope.label: TTS branch
scope.value: Synthesised on the server, never stored

upload.label: Upload branch
upload.value: Played locally; the file has not left the browser

save.title: Create the tag
save.body: Create voice tag saves it and returns you to the list with a confirmation. The new card carries the name, the language flag and the duration measured from the audio itself.
save.mediaHint: The list right after saving, with the new card and the confirmation toast.

result.label: Result
result.value: One tag in your library, ready to use

manage.title: Play it, rename it, or take it to a song
manage.body: On a card, Preview asks for a fresh signed link only when you press it, so opening the tab does not pull audio you were never going to hear. The pencil renames in place — Enter saves, Esc cancels. The bin asks once. When you upload a song, this tag shows up in the picker: search matches without diacritics and forgives a typo.
manage.note: Renaming is the only edit. The audio of a saved tag is fixed — a different take means a new tag.
manage.mediaHint: One card: the preview playing, an inline rename, and the delete dialog.

rename.label: Rename
rename.value: Inline on the card — Enter to save, Esc to cancel

remove.label: Delete
remove.value: Confirmed once, and it is gone

next.title: Song — upload a track and bake the tag in
next.body: Where the loop interval, the tag volume and how far the music ducks underneath are set, and the tagged copy is rendered next to an untouched original.

song.title: Upload a track and bake the tag in.
song.lead: This is where a voice tag stops being a clip and becomes part of a master. Seven steps: pick the file, decide whether it gets a tag, tune how the tag sits under the music, and listen to what comes out.

open.title: Open the Songs tab
open.body: Dashboard → Songs. The list holds every track you have uploaded, with a search box, a status filter and the Upload button. On a fresh account it is empty and points at that same button.
open.note: While any track is still merging, the list refreshes itself every few seconds — you never have to reload to watch a status change.
open.mediaHint: The Songs tab: search box, status filter, Upload button, and the empty state.

file.title: Choose the audio file
file.body: Drop the file on the box or click to browse. The browser reads its length before anything is sent, and fills the title in from the filename — type your own and yours is kept. Change file swaps it without starting the form over.
file.mediaHint: A file just dropped in: name, size, format, length, and the waveform strip.

fork.title: Decide whether it gets a voice tag
fork.body: One checkbox — Attach Voice Tag during upload — splits the rest of the form. Choose carefully: the answer is written into the release and cannot be changed afterwards.

plain.title: Leave it as plain music
plain.body: Skip the checkbox and the track is stored exactly as you uploaded it. Useful for a reference, or for a master you tag somewhere else. Its page and its row both label it plain music afterwards.
plain.mediaHint: The form with the checkbox unticked, showing the three-line explainer.

status.label: Status
status.value: Ready the moment the upload lands

later.label: Want one later
later.value: Upload again with a tag attached

tagged.title: Attach one of your voice tags
tagged.body: Tick the box and the picker appears. From two characters it asks the server, which matches without diacritics and forgives a typo; below that it filters the tags the form already holds. Each row shows the language and the voice, so two tags both called intro stay apart.
tagged.mediaHint: The picker open, with matches, language flags and voice names.

source.label: Source
source.value: The tags you made in module 01

missing.label: No tags yet
missing.value: The form says so and sends you back

tune.title: Tune how the tag sits in the track
tune.body: Four numbers decide the result, each with a slider and a box you can type into. Above them a simulated three-minute timeline marks every insertion as you drag and counts them, so the interval is a picture rather than a guess.
tune.note: Ducking is the one worth reading twice: it is the level the music is held at while the tag speaks, not the amount it drops by. 50% means the music sits at half volume underneath.
tune.mediaHint: Short clip: dragging the interval slider while the timeline markers rearrange.

send.title: Upload, and wait for the merge
send.body: The button walks through four states. It asks for a signed upload link, sends the bytes straight to storage behind a progress bar that follows what actually left your machine, registers the song, then waits for the merge. Only the sending stage can be cancelled — after that the server owns the job.
send.note: Don't want to watch? Run in background hands you to the song's own page, which picks up the same wait. Either way the merge keeps going; closing the tab mid-transfer is what loses it, and the browser warns you before it happens.
send.mediaHint: Short clip: the four phases in order — preparing, uploading with a percentage, finishing, merging.

merge.label: Merging
merge.value: Only with a tag; checked every 2s for up to 5 min

listen.title: Listen to what came out
listen.body: You land on the song's own page. The player decodes the file in the browser to draw the real waveform, not a decoration — click anywhere on it to seek, and loop or change speed from 0.5x to 2x. Under it sits the voice tag configuration the track was built with.
listen.note: Arrived while it was still merging? The banner says so and the page updates itself the moment it finishes. If it failed, the reason is printed and Retry processing queues it again.
listen.mediaHint: The song page: waveform player, status badge, and the read-only configuration grid.

manage.title: Find it again later
manage.body: Back on the list, the pencil renames a track in place and the bin removes it. Search ignores accents and tolerates a typo, so a half-remembered title still lands; the filter narrows to Ready, Processing or Failed when only one of them matters.
manage.note: Deleting takes the original and every processed version with it. The confirmation says as much, and it cannot be undone.
manage.mediaHint: The list with several tracks: an inline rename, the status filter open, and a search result.

rename.label: Rename
rename.value: Inline — Enter to save, Esc to cancel

next.title: Live Room — play it to other people, together
next.body: A six-character code, one track in step for everyone in the room, and voice on top of it.

liveRoom.title: Play it to other people, in the same second.
liveRoom.lead: A room is a six-character code, up to seven people, and one track everybody hears at the same position. Seven steps, split by the role you are in: the host who opens the door, or the guest who knocks.

plan.label: Plan
plan.value: Pro to host, free to join

open.title: Open the Live rooms tab
open.body: Dashboard → Live rooms. The list holds the rooms you own, split into Active and Ended, with search across their names. Two buttons sit above it: Create room, and Join by code.
open.note: Hosting is Pro. Joining someone else's room is not — any signed-in account can walk in with a code, which is what makes a room usable for a client review.
open.mediaHint: The Live rooms list: Active/Ended tabs, a room card with its code and headcount, and both buttons.

fork.title: Open a room, or knock on one
fork.body: The two roles reach the same room from opposite sides. Read the one you are.

host.title: Create the room
host.body: Name it, set how many people it holds and how long it survives you stepping away. The system hands back a six-character code — that code is the whole invitation, and it stays the same for the life of the room.
host.mediaHint: The create form filled in, and the room card that comes back carrying its code.

guest.title: Enter the code
guest.body: Join by code takes six characters and formats them as you type. The lookup answers with the room's name and how full it is before you commit — an ended room says so and stops there. Then you get a camera and microphone check, which you are free to skip.
guest.mediaHint: The code field mid-entry, the lookup result, and the device check with its camera preview.

devices.label: Devices
devices.value: Optional — join without them and turn them on inside

door.title: Ask, and be let in
door.body: Asking to join puts a request in front of the host, who sees it arrive and answers Let in or Decline. Approved, and the guest is pulled into the room automatically after a short countdown they can skip. The room filling up while a request waits declines it on capacity rather than pretending there is space.
door.note: Three declines from the host and that person can no longer ask — the lobby says so instead of letting them keep knocking. Someone already approved once walks straight back in next time, unless they were removed in between.
door.mediaHint: Split view: the host's waiting-to-join queue, and the guest's lobby with its countdown.

approve.label: Let in
approve.value: The guest auto-enters after a countdown

decline.label: Decline
decline.value: Three times locks that person out

inside.title: Look around the room
inside.body: The header carries the room name, the code with a copy button, the headcount and a connection badge that tells you whether you are connected, reconnecting or offline. The video grid rearranges itself by how many people are in — full screen at one, two columns at two, a grid from three up. The bar at the bottom holds camera, microphone, the panel toggles and the way out.
inside.note: A room can only be open in one tab. A second tab on the same room gets a screen offering to jump to the first one or take over, rather than two sessions fighting over one seat.
inside.mediaHint: The room screen with four people: header, video grid, control bar, and the side panel open.

listen.title: Listen to a track together
listen.body: Pick a song and everyone hears it at the same position: the server keeps one playback state per room and stores where the track stood when it started, so each client works out the live position from that plus elapsed time. Play, pause, seek and volume all travel to everybody. Under the waveform, anyone can pin a comment to an exact second — it pops up when playback passes it.
listen.note: The songs offered are the ones in your own library, and only those ready to play — so whoever picks is playing from their own uploads, not the host's. While the host is away the music stays paused for everybody else; only they can start it again.
listen.mediaHint: Short clip: picking a song, the waveform filling, and a comment popping up as playback reaches its second.

source.label: Song source
source.value: The picker's own library, ready tracks only

comments.label: Track comments
comments.value: Up to 200 characters, pinned to a second

moderate.title: Keep the room in order
moderate.body: The People tab is where the host acts. Remove takes somebody out and keeps them out for a cooldown; Mute closes their microphone from across the room and holds it shut for a cooldown, so it cannot be flipped straight back on. Every row shows what state that person's microphone is in and whether their camera is off.
moderate.note: Being removed is not a dead end shown as an error: that person lands on a screen naming what happened, with the wait counting down until they can ask again.
moderate.mediaHint: The People tab with the host's Remove and Mute controls, and the confirmation dialog.

remove.label: Remove
remove.value: Confirmed, then a cooldown before they can return

mute.label: Mute
mute.value: Remote, with a cooldown before they can reopen it

micStates.label: Mic states
micStates.value: On · muted by themselves · muted by the host

end.title: Leave it, or close it
end.body: Leaving and ending are different doors. A guest leaving frees their seat and can walk back in with the same code. The host leaving does not close the room: it holds their seat, tells everybody the host stepped away, and runs down the grace period they set — come back in time and nothing was lost. Ending closes it for everyone with an overlay that says why.
end.note: An ended room is not gone. Reopen keeps the same code and starts a fresh session: the people, the chat and the playback of the previous session do not carry over.
end.mediaHint: The host-stepped-away banner with its countdown, and the Ended tab with a room's Reopen button.

leave.label: Guest leaves
leave.value: Seat freed, same code gets them back

grace.label: Host leaves
grace.value: Seat held, room closes when grace runs out

reopen.label: Reopen
reopen.value: Same code, new session, nothing carried over

technical.title: The three hardest problems, and how they were solved.
technical.lead: Not a stack list. Each case below is a real constraint hit while building, the approach taken, and what had to be given up to take it.

library.title: Moving a 200 MB file without choking the API server
library.subtitle: Direct upload with presigned URLs, and search that survives a typo.
library.problem: Routing the file through the API server means every upload holds a thread and a buffer, and then the same bytes have to travel again to storage. All the user sees is a progress bar that does not move.
library.approach: The backend never touches a byte. It signs a short-lived URL, the browser uploads straight to object storage, and only once that succeeds does the backend write metadata.
library.detail1: Type and size are checked client-side before a URL is requested — a bad file is rejected before any bandwidth is spent.
library.detail2: Progress comes from the XHR progress event, so the percentage is bytes genuinely delivered.
library.detail3: Metadata is written in one transaction after the upload succeeds; a half-finished upload leaves no orphan row.
library.detail4: Search runs on Elasticsearch with an accent-folding analyzer and fuzzy matching, falling back to a PostgreSQL query when Elasticsearch is unreachable.
library.decision: No resumable uploads. Chunking, per-part state and orphan cleanup are three things to maintain forever, in exchange for very little at the scale of a single demo file.

voiceTag.title: Why a tag at 100% still sounded tiny
voiceTag.subtitle: Measure loudness to EBU R128, match the tag to the song, then mix.
voiceTag.problem: A mastered track sits around -9 to -12 LUFS. A voice tag — synthesized, or recorded on whatever the user had — sits around -20 to -27. That 10 to 15 dB gap meant the volume slider ran out of travel long before the tag was audible: 100% only ever meant "unchanged", never "as loud as the song".
voiceTag.approach: Measure the integrated loudness of both sources, work out the gain that puts the tag a fixed headroom above the song, and only then mix. After that the user's percentage finally does what its label promises.
voiceTag.detail1: FFmpeg pipeline: measure LUFS on both → apply gain to the tag → build the looped tag track → mix down to a new file.
voiceTag.detail2: The gain is clamped between −12 dB and +18 dB. Past that the correction does more harm than good: lifting a very quiet tag only surfaces its noise floor.
voiceTag.detail3: Anything below −60 LUFS is treated as unmeasurable rather than believed — near-silence reports a number that would ask for an absurd boost.
voiceTag.detail4: Synthesized and user-recorded voices share one path once they are WAV files; only the source step differs.
voiceTag.decision: Rendered server-side rather than assembled with the Web Audio API in the browser. The result has to be identical on every machine, and the final mix needs to exist as a file to be shareable.

liveRoom.title: Seven people, one track, the same second
liveRoom.subtitle: The server holds an anchor, not a stream. And nobody can listen in on anyone's signalling.
liveRoom.problem: Everyone is on a different connection with different latency, and anyone can reload mid-track. Pushing the playback position every second would be both expensive and still wrong.
liveRoom.approach: The server neither streams audio nor counts seconds. It holds an anchor: which track, at what position, as of when, playing or paused. Each client derives the live position from that anchor plus elapsed time.
liveRoom.detail1: No process ticks every second to write the position — state changes only when somebody presses a button.
liveRoom.detail2: One event carries the whole state; its type only tells a client whether the audio source needs reloading.
liveRoom.detail3: A sequence number on every event makes a late-arriving frame a harmless no-op instead of a jump backwards.
liveRoom.detail4: WebRTC signalling goes through a per-principal user queue rather than a shared topic — one member's SDP and ICE cannot be subscribed to by another.
liveRoom.decision: Ending a room pauses the music instead of clearing it, against the literal requirement. Undo has to restore the session whole — deleting the row would make music the one thing that did not come back.

contact.title: A question, a bug, or an idea — one address for all three.
contact.lead: Everything sent here is read by one person, so write it the way you would to a colleague. If something is broken, the steps you took and what happened instead are the most useful thing you can send.
contact.copyFailed: Could not reach the clipboard — copy the address manually.
contact.responseValue: Usually within one working day, two at the outside.
contact.hoursValue: Vietnam, GMT+7. Anything sent overnight is answered the next morning.
